answer: Shared memory in GPUs (e.g., CUDA-capable devices) is divided into equally sized modules called memory banks, and bank conflicts occur when multiple threads in a warp access different addresses that map to the same memory bank—this happens, for example, when copying a tile from global memory into shared memory. To minimize or avoid these bank conflicts, it is important to understand how memory addresses map to the different memory banks and to schedule memory requests optimally so that concurrent accesses fall into distinct banks rather than colliding on the same one. It's also worth noting that adjusting the shared memory bank size itself does not increase shared memory usage or affect occupancy, so changing bank size configuration is a tool that can be used somewhat independently of memory footprint or occupancy concerns while addressing conflicts.

answer: Coalescing global memory accesses is described as one of the most important performance considerations when programming CUDA-capable GPU architectures, since global memory access efficiency depends heavily on how thread accesses align and combine into memory transactions. If accesses are not properly coalesced—for example, if each thread performs a 4-byte access but this results in a full 32-byte memory transaction being generated per thread rather than combining multiple threads' accesses into a single transaction—much of the transferred data bandwidth is wasted, since only a fraction of the fetched bytes are actually used. This general guidance on coalesced access is covered in the CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide, which provides recommendations for optimizing memory access patterns to achieve better performance on CUDA hardware.
